slices.notes:
One search over everything on a matter, opening scoped to the section the reader is standing on and never widening past the matter. `@magna-carta/matter-search` is a registry of declared read-side sources on the federated timeline's pattern: a source says where its rows live, which capability gates them, and how to project one, and the shared builder composes the matter binding and the visible-matter predicate itself — so a source physically cannot search across matters, and no registered source may name a discovery review table. `GET /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/search` narrows that registry twice before building anything, by the reader's scope and by the capabilities they hold; a withheld source is reported rather than returned empty. The control is `ScreenSearch` with its `scope` seam filled, rendered from the matter layout so every section inherits it, with a panel for the fast path and a results page whose query rides in the address.

Eight sources answer (files by name, time, costs, billing, parties, calendar, notes, custody) against six sections that decline with the line saying what each waits on, and `lint:matter-search-coverage` refuses a section that answers neither way. The registry answers in the section strip's own order, so the answer and the tabs above it never disagree about where things live.

**The load-profile gate has run, and it found one real defect.** The measurement asks the question that decides whether the search can grow: not whether a substring match is fast — it cannot be, and no index makes it so — but whether the MATTER NARROWING is index-served, so the scan reads one case's rows rather than the firm's. The parties source, written as two LEFT JOINs onto the directory, planned a full scan of every entity the firm holds; it now drives from `matter_party` and resolves each name by primary key. Two sources materialise a sort (notes on a computed occurrence date, parties on a case-folded name); both are recorded rather than waved through, because the rows being sorted are rows the scan has already read and bounded by one matter.

**Built is in-progress rather than done, and what remains is no longer ordinary work.** Fees cannot be built at all: a fee is designed as its own dated work-in-progress record and nothing on the wire carries one, so there is nothing to search rather than a source nobody wrote. The matter-asset register is the mirror case — the query is written and reviewed, and it is unregistered because the strip's regrouping left the register with no screen for a hit to land on. File contents wait on a deploy. Everything the schema can answer today, answers. File **contents** are a separate wait — the engine, its write pipeline and its compaction are built, and the port answers `engine-not-implemented` until the search Container is deployed.

Four owner recommendations stand, each reversible and none of them reaching the registry or the route — the snippet within a matter, the `search:matter` key and its broad seeding, per-source rather than global "include deleted", and saying so when a source is withheld.

slices.notes:
Build slice 2·6·1 shipped: the walking slice, template registration through to a filed document.
`@magna-carta/document-assembly` is a pure package over `fflate` + `fast-xml-parser` (the
`@magna-carta/metadata` substrate) holding the guarded OOXML reader/writer, the macro stripper and its
independent re-verification gate, the normalization pass, the declarative merge-field dictionary and
its formatters, the batched resolution pipeline, and the substitution engine. Four per-firm tables
(`document_template`, immutable `document_template_version`, `document_template_field_mapping`,
`document_assembly`), nine catalogue routes plus submit/poll, a `DocumentAssemblyJob` Durable Object
over a dedicated queue, and the assembled document filed through `initiateUpload` /
`completeUploadSession` — the one ingest chokepoint, no bypass. Owner decisions taken: `{{key}}` is
the single stored placeholder form, and the merge is in-house rather than an adopted library.

Both registration transforms of the firm's own document are **opt-in and always reported**, revised
on 2026-08-04 evening. Converting Word merge fields runs only on request, and a template registered
without it keeps them — each recorded on the field manifest with the part it sits in and the frozen
cached text it will print, reported again by every assembly in the response and on the provenance row,
and landing the assembly on `succeeded_with_absences`, so a blank that does not look like a blank
meets the same absence model an ordinary missing value does. Removing macros likewise runs only on
request; a macro-bearing upload without the opt-in is refused with both remedies named, never stored
carrying live macros and never stripped silently. The per-firm **field-mapping library** behind
`MergeFieldNameResolver` is built: confirmed Word-name-to-key mappings written when a conversion
confirms them, read once per registration, listed and deletable under `templates:manage`.

Build slice 2·6·2 shipped the **template expression language** and the three constructs written in it.
`src/expression/` is an OOXML-free folder — `limits.ts`, `errors.ts`, `lex.ts`, `parse.ts`,
`catalog.ts`, `check.ts`, `evaluate.ts` — holding one lexer, one recursive-descent parser over a closed
grammar, one static checker, and one total evaluator, so the language was proven as a language before it
met a package. A merge key is ONE lexical atom resolved by exact match through a `Map`, there is no
production for property traversal, indexing, assignment, a lambda, a regular expression, or a call to
anything but a frozen helper allowlist, and nothing in the folder throws. Lex, parse, name-resolve,
type-check, format-check, and limit-check all run at REGISTRATION, so a type error is a registration
failure with a part, an excerpt, and a character offset inside the expression — never an assembly
surprise. The manifest stores each block's and computed field's SOURCE rather than a tree, and assembly
re-checks from it, which is what catches dictionary drift.

`{{#if}}` / `{{#unless}}` / `{{#each}}` / `{{= }}` operate on whole paragraphs and whole table rows —
a marker in a row's first cell makes the row the unit — so list numbering and table banding survive a
removed or a repeated unit, and every repeat clone carries its own paragraph and row properties. Money
arithmetic is integer-exact through `@magna-carta/money`, with every intermediate checked before the
operation so the package's own guard is unreachable; division is not an operator, and `divideExact`,
`divideRounded`, `applyRate`, `percentOf`, and `allocate` each state their rounding. Owner-flagged
defaults applied as recommended: an unresolved condition FAILS the assembly naming the field (G1),
banker's rounding only (G2), no business-day math (G3), no pronoun helper (G5). G4 was answered the
following day the other way: `sum`, `minimum`, and `maximum` fold a LITERAL FIELD PATH of a list-valued
key, bounded by exactly what a repeat is bounded by — one batched read, the items-per-repeat cap, a
step per element — with an empty collection left unresolved rather than answered zero, because a
smallest of nothing has no answer and a total of no amounts has no currency. `matter.parties` is the
first list-valued source, one batched read for the whole collection.

The security claim carries its fuzz obligation in the slice: a seeded structure-aware generator over
the grammar, a seeded byte-level generator, a committed denied-construct corpus that must fail at parse
or check and never at evaluation, a pretty-print-and-reparse property (which found a real precedence
bug), an independent BigInt arithmetic oracle, and one bound-hitting test per declared limit.

The **custom-field merge bindings and the letterhead logo** shipped next. A firm's own matter-axis
fields enter the dictionary at read time as `custom.<customField_ handle>` entries derived from
`custom_field` — bound by handle and never by name, so a rename breaks nothing — with the catalogue
read once (`readCustomFieldCatalog`) and shared by registration, the field-list surface, and assembly,
which is what makes drift detectable rather than silent: an archived field contributes no entry, so a
template bound to it fails naming the key, and a stored value behind an archived field is skipped and
reported as an absence. Values resolve through one statement covering every handle, joining the
picklist option's label and the referenced record's display name rather than fetching either per value.
`effectiveNumberScale` is REUSED from `@magna-carta/custom-fields` rather than restated, so the same
stored `500` is five hundred on a number field and five dollars on a currency field, and a currency
field with a non-currency scale renders as the exact decimal it is instead of as wrong-looking money.
The hard-delete guard gained its template-binding arm: a field a template manifest names is
`field-in-use` and routes to Archive, with `document_template_version` referenced by string so the
sibling packages stay independent. `custom.customField_…` also lexes as ONE atom in the expression
language — a handle's alphabet includes the hyphen, which is also subtraction, so the atom is matched by
its exact fixed length and no author's spacing can decide which it is.

The **letterhead logo** is the engine's first image work, and answers the design's open question 3:
**the asset declares the box**. `location` gained the logo columns (object key, sniffed content type,
size, hash, intrinsic pixels, printed width in EMU); only a width is stored, so the height follows from
the intrinsic aspect ratio and no document can print a stretched mark. `PUT`/`DELETE
/api/v1/locations/{id}/letterhead-logo` take the image inline (a firm's mark is tens of kilobytes, and
one request is the only shape where reading what the bytes are, measuring them, and writing the row
that points at them happen together). `src/ooxml/image.ts` emits all four halves of a picture — the
part, the `[Content_Types].xml` Default, the relationship on the drawing part (ids allocated per part,
by scanning the ids present), and the inline `w:drawing` with every namespace bound on the element that
uses it — and `packageIntegrityViolations` now proves each one over the emitted bytes, because a
document whose words are right and whose picture wiring is not is a document no reader opens and no
text assertion catches. **Image-format policy: PNG and JPEG only, decided by magic bytes rather than by
a declared content type**, enforced at the write and re-checked at assembly; SVG, EMF/WMF, GIF, BMP and
TIFF are refused with the reasoning recorded. An office with no logo, or one whose object has gone,
assembles with a visible marker.

The **load-profile volume profile** deferred by all three build slices is now in the harness. A
`documentAutomation` volume lays down the firm's template catalogue with its immutable version history,
an archived tail, the confirmed Word-name-to-merge-key mapping library, and the assembly provenance
rows — every write through the real composed effects, never a raw insert — plus, on one probe matter
deliberately chosen NOT to be the custom-field measurements' own probe, the merge-context hot case: the
firm's own matter-axis fields with current values, and a full party list. At the committed baseline
that is 181 templates over 479 versions with 27 archived, 1,605 assemblies, 120 mapping rows, and a
probe matter carrying 40 custom-field values and 13 party links.

The four measured operations the design names are on the clock: the catalogue list taken at a real
keyset boundary rather than at the head of the table, the one-read current-version resolve every job
starts with, the whole batched merge context for the widest template the firm's dictionary can offer,
and the custom-field manifest read the dictionary is derived from. **Every hot-path plan is an index
walk — the scan allowlist for this set is empty.** The read the design flagged as the likely table-wide
exception, the firm's field catalogue, walks `custom_field_scope_index` instead. What the merge-context
measurement is really for is the batching rule: its cost tracks the number of SOURCES, not the number
of fields, so a per-field resolver reintroduced later shows up as a curve rather than as a code review.

The declared-field count per template version is bounded by the dictionary rather than by the profile:
a manifest field is keyed by its merge key, so the probe template declares every key the firm has for
that matter — every platform key the dictionary carries (17 at the time it was laid down, 29 once the
Directory role sources landed) plus its 40 custom bindings. The number the batching rule is about is the
40-handle bound-parameter list of the one value statement, and that is the parameter the profile carries;
the platform half widens whenever the dictionary does, without moving the read count.

The **Directory role sources** shipped next, closing the first of the two named seams. Four
platform-declared roles — `opposingParty`, `opposingCounsel`, `guardian`, `witness` — each contribute a
name, a person-or-organisation kind, and a `<role>.all` collection, so a caption names the opposing party
the way it already names the client and a repeat lists them all. The set is PLATFORM-DECLARED rather than
derived from the firm's `directory_party_role` catalogue: a custom field binds by a minted handle
precisely because its name is firm-typed text, and a role has no handle — only the words a firm typed,
which neither lex as one atom nor get typed from memory. Matching is by normalization instead, both sides
lowercased with every non-alphanumeric character removed, so `opposing_party`, `Opposing Party`, and
`opposing-party` are one role and no two shipped sources may normalize alike (a fitness test, not care).
**Ambiguity is an answer:** a matter linking three opposing parties resolves the singular keys to nothing
and says there were three, rather than taking the first by created-at — a document naming the wrong
defendant is the mistake nobody catches by reading it. The reason rides a new `absenceReasons` channel on
the merge context through to `AssemblyAbsence.reason` and into the failure text of a condition that could
not be worked out, and is deliberately NOT persisted: the provenance row records absent KEYS, and a count
of a matter's parties is the matter's data. No new read — every role is derived from the party collection
the merge context already fetched, so a template naming four roles costs what one naming none did, and
the four measured plans are untouched index walks.

**Protected-value binding** closed the second named seam, and closed it by extending the existing decrypt
path rather than by building beside it. The client's sealed Directory identifiers — Social Security
number, Employer Identification Number, date of birth, driver's license number, account number, and
SSN-last-four — are dictionary entries carrying `sensitivity: protected`, which is the ROUTING decision
and not a label: they resolve through an injected reader wired to the directory's `readIdentifier`, which
is `readProtected` — permission gate, decrypt-audit row committed before any plaintext, AAD-bound
decrypt, inseparable. `@magna-carta/document-assembly` names no ciphertext column, derives no key, and
decrypts nothing; the refusal it turns into an absence is the chokepoint's own
`ProtectedReadForbiddenError`, caught by identity so the gate is never restated. **No assembly-specific
audit shape:** the same `protected.decrypt` event, the same subject (the identifier row the AAD binds
to), the same table a direct read writes — recorded as an ADR, since the alternative was a second reason
code and a firm's "who saw this value" answer split across two shapes.

**A member without the permission gets the document.** The field lands on the absence model with a reason
naming the field and the permission, the draft shows the usual visible marker, and the assembly completes
`succeeded_with_absences`; nothing is thrown, and the plaintext exists nowhere on that path. Permissions
are RE-DERIVED when the job runs rather than carried on the queue message, so a revoked grant bites — the
message carries an identity, never a decided answer — and the read is deferred to the first protected key,
so an ordinary template pays nothing. The decrypt count is bounded by the manifest rather than batched
(each ciphertext is bound to its own row and commits its own audit record, so a bulk form would have to
bypass the chokepoint to exist): one decrypt per protected key the manifest names, deduplicated, and a
refusal costs exactly one attempt. The subject rides the party read that already happens; a matter linking
no single client decrypts nothing and says how many it links. Both field-list surfaces now carry an
entry's sensitivity, so an author sees what a template has bound before anything is assembled —
registration itself is unrestricted, because binding names a key, not a value.

A firm declaring one of its OWN fields protected is a separate decision and not this one: it needs a
column on `custom_field` and a ciphertext column on `custom_field_value` that do not exist, and the
derivation in `custom-field-bindings.ts` is the one line that reads the declaration once they do.

Build slice 2·6·5 shipped **the generated catalogue and its contract** — the substrate the merge-field
catalogue grows on. The dictionary is no longer a hand-written array: it is the cross product of a
SUBJECT registry (the things a document can talk about) with a FACET registry (the facts a subject of
that kind carries), plus the written-out facts of the one-of-a-kind subjects. `DIRECTORY_ROLE_SOURCES`
folds into the subject registry rather than living beside it, so adding a party role is one row whose
whole facet set follows and adding a facet is one row every subject of that kind gains with identical
absence behaviour, formats, and description wording. A hand-written catalogue's wrong row is seen by
nobody; a generated one's is wrong on every subject at once and is seen by every test together, which is
the trade the shape makes and the reason the fitness functions below exist.

**A committed golden key list makes permanence a property rather than a promise.**
`test/fixtures/shipped-keys.json` records every shipped key with its value type, source, default
rendering, absence behaviour, and sensitivity; the test fails when a key disappears, changes any of
them, or makes its absence LESS visible (`blank` → `placeholder` → `fail` is the one permitted
direction). Adding a key stays safe — a template cannot bind what did not exist — and stays deliberate:
it lands as a diff to that file. Two keys were added this way, `client.kind` and `client.all`, which the
client subject gains from the party facet set.

**Presentation lives on the dictionary entry**, so the read contract is its projection rather than its
twin. Every entry carries a label, a picker heading from a declared group registry, the subject it is
about, a prominence, search synonyms, and one example rendering per legal format — produced by running
an invented sample through the REAL format table, so an example can never describe a rendering the
formatter does not produce. Availability and its note are DERIVED from the source and the subject's
optionality rather than declared on every row. The absence marker reads the label, so a missing opposing
counsel leaves `[OPPOSING COUNSEL'S NAME]` rather than `[OPPOSING COUNSEL DISPLAY NAME]`.

**The structured `name` value type** rides along, because it is what makes the format system testable:
`displayName` carries the parts the Directory records — projected on the party read that already happens,
not a new one — and gains `full`, `formal`, `lastFirst`, `initials`, `family`, `given`, and `upper`. Its
default rendering is byte-for-byte the string it always printed, proven against the plain-text rendering
of the same recorded string, so no registered template's output moved. A RENDERING THE RECORD CANNOT
SUPPORT IS A DECLARED ABSENCE WITH A REASON naming the missing part — never a fallback to a different
rendering, which is the same failure the ambiguity rule refuses one level up.

**The field-binding index** (`document_template_field_binding`) is the one new table: one row per
distinct merge key a version's manifest names, written in the same batch as the version. A template
version is immutable, so the rows can never disagree with the manifest they came from — no update path,
no reconciliation, no staleness mode. It turns the custom-field hard-delete guard's `instr()` scan over
every stored manifest into an index seek, and it is what "where is this field used" and the picker's
usage ordering will read. `documentTemplate.fieldBinding` counts the write by outcome; no merge-field key
is ever a dimension.

Load profile: the `documentAutomation` set gains the catalogue projection and the binding-index lookup,
both index walks, with the generator version bumped because registration now writes binding rows.

**Slices 2·6·8–2·6·10 built and tested — the platform record subjects, unblocked by the owner's H1
ratification.** Three per-firm records land as the Matters area's own tables with the catalogue as one
consumer: `matter_assignment` (staffing beyond the responsible attorney, whose one home stays the
matter row — an assignment role that normalizes to it is refused), `matter_court_case` (the court a
Directory organisation, the judge a Directory person, the case number and the two caption designation
words — side is a recorded fact, never a key axis), and `matter_estate` (the decedent a Directory
person, the styles STORED exactly as the court fixed them, never composed). `matter_party` gains a
recorded `capacity`, and the member professional profile carries title, admissions, direct dial, and
professional email — written through `firm:manageMembers` until the platform grows a self-scoped
mutation concept (the deferral the pending decision record names).

Fifty-five keys on three new batched reads — five member subjects on one staffing read, `court.*` and
`case.*` on one court-case read, `estate.*` on one estate read — and the whole-catalogue read budget
grows from four statements to seven. The member subjects share the party facet grammar (level-1
ambiguity naming the count, `.all` as the way out) and every name is parts-carrying, so all seven
renderings apply to an attorney, the judge, and the decedent alike. `<member>.barNumber` is the first
protected fact about the firm's own people: `bar_number` joins the Directory identifier catalog
(protected, never standalone-indexed), resolves only through the chokepoint reader, and is never
attempted for a slot that resolved ambiguously — proven end to end in the worker suite with the audit
table itself (value plus one audit row with the permission; marker plus reason and NO row without it;
no row at all on an ambiguous slot, even for a member who holds the permission). `capacityLine`
composes in the resolver from three recorded facts with ONE absence naming the missing part — the

**Build slice 2·6·3 shipped its first half — PDF output, and the shape the signature hand-off needs.**
An assembly takes an optional `outputFormat`; the `pdf` arm hands the merged package to the registry's
own `docx`-to-`pdf` edge inside the same job, through the same `runConversion` and the same
per-engine-id resolver the file-converter tool executes with. Document automation contributes no
engine, no adapter, and no registry entry — the office suite already had exactly this job, and a
second path to a PDF would be a second answer to what a firm's letterhead looks like on paper.
Converting through the file-converter tool instead was the alternative and was declined: its artifact
is transient, expires, and is never filed, so the member would download and re-upload and the matter
would carry a document nothing connects to the assembly that made it.

**A conversion that cannot be done fails the assembly (`conversion-failed`); nothing is filed.** The
substitution it refuses — file the word-processing package and warn — produces a document that reads
as the one that was asked for and is discovered to be wrong at the moment somebody tries to sign it,
which is the absence model's own failure one level up. The requested format is a COLUMN
(`document_assembly.output_format`, additive, `docx` default) rather than something read off the filed
object, because the two cases that need the answer are a job still queued and a job that failed, and
neither has an object to read. The poll answers it beside the file and version handles from the moment
of submit.

**That recorded format is the whole of the signature hand-off on the backend, and deliberately so.**
The design named the hand-off a link rather than a build, and it is what the platform can honestly
support: `POST /api/v1/documents/seal` is a stateless operation over PDF bytes, and there is no
envelope, signer-invitation, or consent-disclosure model on `main` for an out-for-signature workflow
to hang from. So an assembled document now arrives in the one shape the seal accepts and says that it
has; a signing ceremony surface is planned rather than invented, because a consent disclosure is a
legal artifact and guessing at one is worse than not offering the button. The Documents surface gains
the format choice and records the PDF arm as `deployed-only` in its availability inventory — the
office suite runs in a container the convert worker owns, which is a deploy-time activation, and a
person on a developer's machine is told that rather than left to conclude the feature is broken.
Fillable-PDF form templates and the signing surface are written into
[`docs/specs/2026-08-13-document-automation-tail-remainder-plan.md`](../docs/specs/2026-08-13-document-automation-tail-remainder-plan.md)
rather than half-built.

**Fillable-PDF form templates shipped as a template KIND rather than a second subsystem.**
`document_template_version.kind` is `wordProcessing | pdfForm`, defaulting to the existing value, and
the two kinds share the catalogue, the immutable version ladder, the ingest gate, the field-manifest
shape, the binding index, the per-firm dictionary, the formatters, the absence model, the provenance
row, and the telemetry — while sharing no engine. `prepareFormTemplateVersion` reads the AcroForm field
set through an injected reader (`crates/pdf-core` behind `@magna-carta/pdf`, so the domain package stays
pure TypeScript), scrubs the upload, and builds the manifest from the SCRUBBED bytes; `fillFormTemplate`
plans the fill and hands it to the same engine. The assembly job branches in exactly one place, and
everything either side of the branch is shared.

**A box binds only what a human confirmed, and the exact name match is refused too.** A mapping comes
from the registration request or from the firm's existing `document_template_field_mapping` library —
the same store the Word `MERGEFIELD` conversion writes to. A field whose name IS a merge key character
for character is reported as a proposal and nothing applies it: a proposal built on exactness becomes
one built on normalization and then on resemblance, and the line has to sit where it fits in one
sentence. Every terminal field the form declares comes out either bound or on a fourth manifest list
(`unboundFormFields`) with its reason — `no-confirmed-mapping`, `not-fillable`, or `unclassified` — and
a field the engine cannot classify is never filled as text, because a text fill writes an appearance
stream and an appearance stream prints. A form that binds nothing warns that every document from it is
the blank form, which is the failure `FORMTEXT` and the placeholder-showing content control each
produced before their lists existed. The absence model is unchanged, with one honest divergence: a tick
box and a set-answer box have nowhere to print a marker, so an unanswerable one is left unanswered with
the reason recorded rather than ticked.

**Flatten-or-not is left open as a typed seam rather than decided.** `FormFillFinish` is a REQUIRED
parameter on the fill, and the platform's one answer is a named constant in the worker's engine wiring,
`interactive` while the question is open — flattening is irreversible and a flattened form cannot be
corrected, so the non-destructive option is what sits behind an unanswered owner decision. Answering it
is a one-line change to that constant, or a change from a constant to a per-template column read. A
curated jurisdiction court-form library stays out of scope: these are the forms a firm supplies.

Named but not fixed, in an area this slice does not own: `crates/pdf-core`'s sanitizer removes metadata,
attachments, the XFA dataset, field values, the structure tree, bookmarks, and optional content, but not
document-level JavaScript or additional actions — so a fillable PDF is not made inert the way the OOXML
macro strip makes a `.docx` inert, and there is no consent gate matching the macro one. What stands
between a hostile form and a firm today is the scan every uploaded byte already crosses, run over the
stored bytes at registration.

slices.notes:
Tantivy keyword search over immutable per-firm splits in R2 — a split is a self-contained segment bundle plus a footer, so a query prunes on footers and range-reads only the postings it walks, making per-query I/O scale with query selectivity rather than corpus size. Built: the pure-Rust engine core (`crates/search-core`, a read-only `Directory` over a `RangeReader`), the per-firm `index_split` catalog and its data-access statements, the `SearchIndexPort` with typed outcomes, keyword/hybrid query composition with reciprocal rank fusion, and the **write pipeline** — a `SearchIndexJob` Durable Object over a dead-lettered queue that turns each committed document version into one split at a derived, content-addressed key, so a retry converges instead of duplicating. Extraction is composite and decided per page: the document's own text layer is read natively in
`crates/pdf-core` and only the pages that have none go to recognition, with per-page `native`/`ocr`
provenance on the result — which is what makes a born-digital PDF searchable at all, and what lets a
mixed document (a scan appended to a contract) extract both halves. A daily re-extraction sweep
re-enqueues any committed current version the catalog holds no live split for, so documents recorded
unreadable by the earlier recognition-only extractor are repaired without a marker or a migration.
**Compaction** is built: the engine merges many splits into one at segment level (the schema does not
store `body`, so a re-index is not available and a segment merge is both the only option and the cheaper
one), applying the delete set inside the merge so superseded postings leave the published bytes. It is
triggered by a live-split threshold the write path notices in one indexed count, single-flighted per
corpus by a Durable Object, bounded by count and bytes with self-re-enqueue so a large back-catalogue
converges, and backstopped by the daily cron. Publication is object, then one atomic catalog batch, then
nothing: superseded source objects are retired by a later sweep after a grace period, which is what keeps
an in-flight query from ever holding a key to bytes that are gone. A new per-firm `index_split_member`
table records what a merged split covers, so a re-indexed document's stale version is excluded per split
until the next merge repacks it out. The engine also now holds a split open across queries and answers a
ranged multi-split query — the two absences the read-path benchmark named, both of which the benchmark
now measures. Gated per firm by `search.indexing_enabled` (off by default) and enqueued off the clean
ingest commit. The engine now reaches real storage. `containers/search` wraps the crate in an axum service whose
`HttpRangeReader` costs one HEAD to open a split and exactly one closed-`Range` GET per read the engine
makes; `apps/search-worker` owns that Container with `enableInternet` false and intercepts its object
calls into the app Worker, so the engine reads a firm's index while holding no credential for it; and the
app Worker's split-object host verifies a per-operation, corpus-scoped HMAC capability token, resolves
the firm's bucket through the one home for that decision, refuses an unranged GET rather than serving a
split whole, and stamps a published split with its object dimensions. Deferred deliberately: the
container keeps no split cache between calls (a cached searcher answers from bytes authorized on an
earlier call, and the residency sizing needs a resident corpus to measure), so a first query pays its
opens against object storage rather than local disk — the read counts are the same either way.

key, with the two channels composing in opposite directions (the firm's tier is a floor in app, the
member's choice wins by email); the mandatory in-app floor on `security` and `trust` from either

firm preference API. **Deviation:** the plan's `notification_delivery` row with
`suppressed_reason = 'not-visible'` at fan-out is not built — the column is `NOT NULL` against a
recipient row that by definition does not exist, and deciding visibility at fan-out is the
emission-time enforcement this subsystem refuses. The designated member gets an ordinary recipient

Slice 4 built: the email digest — the first time this subsystem hands anything to a mailbox, and the
first consumer of slice 3's per-category email cadence. A digest window read added to the ONE shared
read the feed and the unread count already compose, so the wall binds at delivery time in one
implementation; a keyset watermark (an instant AND its event id) per member per cadence; a renderer
whose entire vocabulary is a closed category label, an integer, a cadence and a configured origin, so
there is no argument a title could arrive in; and an hourly per-firm run anchored to the firm's own
morning, resolved from the default office the calendar already books against rather than a second
copy of where the firm is. Send first, mark second, both committed in one batch. A member with
nothing visible in the window gets no email. **Every row a run did not mail is settled** as a
`suppressed` `notification_delivery` row naming a closed reason — `preference` where the member's
cadence for that category is `off` or the resolved detail level is `off`, `no-address` where there is
no mailbox — so a member who chose not to be written to stays distinguishable from a member the
platform silently failed to write to, which is the in-app suppression tally's requirement met with
the mechanism the schema already had.

**Deviation 1 — the immediate escalation.** The plan's task 4.3 asks the run to honour a
registry-declared `escalation: "immediate"` for trust and security kinds. No registered kind declares

untriggered code while leaving such kinds in the digest would quietly mail a compliance-grade notice
inside a day's counts. Built instead: the walk HALTS at the first such row, leaving the watermark
behind it so nothing is settled that no channel carried, and a fitness test asserts no type declares
`immediate` today. Registering the first one is a gate failure until its send path ships.
`emailContent: 'recipient-scoped'` gets the same treatment for the same reason.

**Deviation 2 — the send port.** The digest resolves its own rather than reusing `emailAdapterForEnv`,
which falls back to the dev logging adapter when the Email Service binding is absent. Right for a
password reset; catastrophic here, because the run would record `sent` rows and advance watermarks
for mail printed to a log, and the member would never hear about those notifications again. The
digest port reports one of three typed not-configured reasons instead, counted every pass.

**Not built, deliberately:** any `apps/web` change. An email template is not a screen, and the

**Repaired in passing:** the per-firm drizzle snapshot had fallen one migration behind the schema
(the discovery processing-route migration was hand-written without refreshing it), so the next

**Slice 4 — what the dedupe key actually guarantees, resolved and named.** A correctness question
raised against the shipped subsystem: the UNIQUE index that makes a notification fire once lives on
`notification_event.dedupe_key`, and the retention sweep deletes that row, so the uniqueness that
enforces "once" does not outlive the firm's window. Settled as **the intended contract, not a defect**,
on the subsystem's own evidence: the design spec frames the key as a redelivery floor throughout (path
A "a redelivery is a no-op by construction", path B raising "once per day" in as many words), and each
production path's required lifetime is far shorter than the thirty-day retention floor — an outbox row
is published once and flipped out of `pending` so the relay never re-carries it, a comparison's bucket
is derived from the pass's own instant so it only ever moves forward, and a job reports each terminal
state once inside its own life. No shipped consumer relies on forever semantics, and the platform
already routes conditions that need it away from this key: the billing automations put their
convergence in `invoice_reminder` rows for exactly this reason and wrote down why.

So nothing durable was built. What was wrong was that the boundary lived only in another subsystem's
design document while the code said "dedupe key" and "UNIQUE" and left the reader to infer "once,
ever". The horizons are now declared per production path in `CONVERGENCE_HORIZON_BY_RAISER`, as a
`Record<NotificationRaisedBy, …>` so a fourth path is a **compile error** until it states one; both
`materialize.ts` and `retention.ts` name the boundary and the rule that follows it (a condition needing
once-per-subject-forever convergence carries it in the owning subsystem's own tables and points a
notification at that record); and `test/retention-convergence.test.ts` states the semantics out loud by
re-inserting a key the sweep took, then proves the property that makes it safe — the comparison bucket
follows the clock, so a swept bucket is unreachable rather than merely unlikely.

**One real hole closed beside it.** The comparison pass's per-kind findings cap was already counted
(`notifications.comparison_clamped`, over-reading by one to detect rather than infer). Its **zone
discovery** was not. The deadline comparison needs one cutoff per zone because no D1 query resolves a
zone, and that read was bounded at the same 200 with no over-read and no counter — so a truncated zone
list meant every deadline in an undiscovered zone matched neither the overdue bound nor the due-today
window, and the pass reported nothing about a whole jurisdiction with every other counter reading
healthy. It now over-reads by one and reports `notifications.comparison_zone_discovery_truncated`, kept
apart from the findings clamp because a clamp bounds what was missed and this does not bound it at all.
The value counts truncated **passes** rather than zones, because a read that over-reads by one to catch
its own truncation learns that it truncated and can never learn by how much.

**Left to the owner, not shipped:** whether 200 findings per kind per pass is the right ceiling. It is
counted rather than silent, but a busy litigation practice can exceed it honestly, and raising it
changes how much of a firm's overdue work gets reported — a firm-observable change and a load question,
recorded on the `notifications.scheduling` ledger node.

**Slice 3 gap closed — the firm's half of the settings had no writer.** A mechanical scan for exported
write-shaped functions with no production caller found three of them in this package, all in one
subsystem: the FIRM tier of the preference matrix (the in-app floor a member may not lower), the
retention window, and the digest local hour. Every one is read at evaluation time — the floor by the
shared recipient resolver on every fan-out, the window by the nightly sweep, the hour by the hourly
digest pass — and no route wrote any of them, so the floor could not be raised, the window could not
be changed and the summary landed at 07:00 for every firm on earth. The member API shipped; the firm
API did not, and the tests that covered the floor inserted the row themselves, which is why nothing
failed. Now `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/notifications/policy` under a new
`firm:manageNotificationPolicy` seeded to Owner/Admin — deliberately not the member key
`notifications:read`, which every default role including Read-only carries. Still not written by
anything: the firm's email DETAIL-LEVEL ceiling, which has no write statement in either tier and is a
separate gap rather than an omission here.

slices.notes:
**Sub-slices 1 and 2 built.** Sub-slice 1 — trust schema, the three-level client/matter tree, the zero floor written in the creation batch, the composition guard owning no-commingling and fees-never-touch-trust, holds and available balance, the two-linked-entry transfer, and the fitness suite. Fifteen owner flags stay open; the code refuses rather than defaults wherever one would have to be guessed.

**Sub-slice 2** — deposits, disbursements, and matter-to-matter transfers, each behind a required-idempotency route; the append-only `trust_movement` client-ledger record carrying source or payee, purpose, method-as-a-value, reference, and the authorizing member, with its shape enforced by a database CHECK; available balance as the disbursement ceiling; a bank-free reallocation between two matters of one client; and a movement refusal on an account whose office recorded no jurisdiction. The jurisdiction corpus remains open.

**The matter-close gate** is the matter shell's close hook filled for the first time: a matter whose client trust ledger still holds money, or carries an active disputed-funds hold, is refused with the balance, the account holding it, and the movements that clear it. Rules are handed to the shell by the composition root rather than imported by it, and a rule may also guard the close batch itself, so a deposit landing between the check and the commit aborts the close instead of slipping under it. A matter with no trust ledger closes freely.

**Two-person disbursement authorization** (owner-directed) closes the last open piece of sub-slice 2: a disbursement is a pending request until a second member approves it, and the movement posts only on that approval, with the approver as `authorized_by` and the submitter as `recorded_by`. The approver-differs rule is a database trigger, not route discipline; the available-balance ceiling is re-read at approval time through the same composer an ungated payment used, so a request overtaken by other activity refuses instead of posting; rejection and withdrawal are recorded, append-only, alongside the request. A firm with a single member holding `trust:manage` may still pay, with that basis stated on the record, and the database withdraws the exception the moment a second such member exists. Three recommended defaults are flagged for owner review: every disbursement is gated rather than only those over a threshold, a pending request never expires, and no new permission was minted.

**The Nevada jurisdiction corpus** fills the jurisdiction seam for the first time, and it still refuses. Nevada's rules are read out of the state's own published text — retention, the IOLTA regime, overdraft notification, unclaimed funds, annual compliance, and advance-fee treatment — with every value carrying the citation and the verbatim sentence it came from, because a value the reviewing attorney cannot check against the rule is a value they cannot review. Encoded is not verified: a profile with no recorded attorney review refuses every requirement with its own code, distinct from the never-researched refusal and from the no-office-state one, and the review binds to the profile revision it was performed against so an amendment re-closes the gate rather than inheriting an attestation about superseded text. Nevada ships NOT VERIFIED, and the read that surfaces the profile with its citations never throws — a firm shown nothing has no reason to get anything reviewed. Every other jurisdiction stays not-encoded with no baseline behind it. Three facts this repository had already written down turned out to be wrong against the current rules, all traceable to the State Bar's own 2019 handbook: retention is five years and not seven, the account-mechanics rule is SCR 78 and not the repealed SCR 78.5, and Nevada mandates no reconciliation at any cadence — the approved schema design's golden test for Nevada would have locked the last two in. The bank-charge carve-out is encoded as a cited rule and deliberately not wired: Nevada permits it, states no cap, and exempts pooled accounts from the charges it would pay, so the permission sits beside a composition guard that still refuses firm money in trust. Flags T7 and T8 shipped as owner-ratified; the attorney review itself and three research caveats are listed for the owner.

**The authorization policy** (owner-directed) turns the always-two-person rule into the firm's own posture: off, threshold (a second person for amounts strictly above a stated amount), or always, plus an independent option requiring whoever lets money go to hold the new `trust:authorize` capability — authority encoded as a capability predicate, seeded to Owner/Admin and Attorney, never a role name. The shipped default is the strict posture as an absent row, so nothing relaxes on migrate; a change is a new append-only version requiring `trust:authorize`, audited from-and-to. Every request stamps the version current at submission and is decided under that stamp — an in-flight request keeps its policy in both directions — and the earned-fee application follows the same policy through the same queue: an application is a request of kind `earned_fee_application` whose invoice lines billing keeps beside it, approved through billing, posting the transfer, the invoice applications, and the decision as one batch. Basis exactness (`second_person` / `sole_trust_manager` / `policy_exempt`), the authority requirement, the stamp itself, and the transfer's recorded actors are all database triggers. Flagged for the owner: whether relaxing the posture should itself take a second person, and whether matter-to-matter reallocations should fall under the policy.

**Review-gate hardening and the catalog re-verification** land the corpus follow-ups before the port is bound or any attorney review is recorded. A review now binds to a content-derived revision — the authored date plus a fingerprint of everything the reviewer attests to — so an amendment that forgets the revision bump closes the gate rather than silently inheriting the attestation. The two newer refusals (encoded-but-unreviewed, and a reviewed jurisdiction's unresearched field) map to the jurisdiction-unavailable problem type with their siblings instead of the generic catch-all; a source-scan fitness guard trips any future surface that computes on an unreviewed value through the display seam; and the silence-resolved singletons are frozen against caller mutation. The narrative 56-jurisdiction catalog was swept against the primary-source records: the Nevada entry's repealed SCR 78.5 citations are corrected, its unclaimed-funds facts aligned with NRPC 1.15(f) and the NRS 120A.500(6)(f) exemption, and the 55 sibling entries — which no primary source in the repository can check — are banner-marked NOT VERIFIED, research leads rather than findings.

**Three-way reconciliation** closes sub-slice 4. A bank statement is a recorded period with its lines — entered by a member, or imported from a file through a preview that reports what it found and stores nothing until a separate confirmation quotes that report's fingerprint back. Statement lines are tied to recorded ledger entries by a person: the platform ranks bounded candidates and shows the reasons, and nothing anywhere records a match on its own. The proof ties three totals as of the period end — the statement's closing balance adjusted for outstanding items, the trust bank account's book balance, and the sum of the client ledgers — both ledger legs computed from dated rows rather than a stored balance, so a period reproduces. Unmatched lines and unmatched recorded items are named outcomes rather than errors, and a proof that does not tie out records which leg disagrees and by how much rather than being forced green. Closing freezes the proof on an append-only row the database refuses to reopen; an unbalanced period closes recording exactly that, and a correction is a new reconciliation superseding the old. The load profile gained the trust volume — the sub-ledger tree, movements, holds, two years of monthly statements each carrying an unrecorded service charge, and the reconciliations over them — with the three-way computation and the client-ledger reads measured against index-walk plans. Flags T9, T10, and T11 shipped as the analysis's recommended defaults and are listed for owner review.

**Authority-based authorization** (owner-directed) reshapes the posture the policy expresses: authority is a property of the person, not a count of people. A member holding `trust:authorize` releases money out of a client ledger — or takes earned fees against a finalized bill — alone and in ONE atomic act (the request, the movement, and the decision recording the footing ride one batch), and a member without it raises the same payment and is told, before composing anything, who can settle it. The shipped posture is now that rule as DATA: a per-firm migration seeds version 1 (`off` plus the authority requirement) conditionally on the table being empty, so the absent-row reading stays strict for the requests it describes, no shipped trigger is touched, and a firm that already chose a posture keeps it. A firm wanting a ceiling still writes a `threshold` or `always` version; above the ceiling the authority requirement binds whichever of the two decides, which is peer approval with no new setting and no new mirror. The one addition is `resolveTrustAuthorizationDisposition`, a read in front of the guarantees that both money-out paths choose solo-versus-route from — it calls the existing predicate rather than restating it, asks the authority question first and always of the ACTOR, and fails closed on an unrecognized kind. The lone-holder count-plus-membership pair is extracted into one helper all three TypeScript callers share. Flagged for the owner: the exception still counts `trust:manage` rather than `trust:authorize` (the design's open question 1, left open because the change would relax a firm with several managers and one authority holder), and the seed relaxes any firm that exists today with no policy row from always-two-person to authority-solo. UI deferred.

**The bank-charge carve-out** (owner flag T3, owner-directed "wire it narrowly") gives a trust bank account somewhere to put the one item on a real bank statement that no member authorized. The firm's own funds go in for the single purpose the conduct rules permit, and the narrowness is structural in five independent places rather than stated as policy: the record lives in its own table with **no column for a client, a matter, a node, or a payee**, so a row of it cannot describe a movement of anybody else's money; the entry goes through a second composition door admitting exactly the firm-funds balance paired with its own account's bank leaf, while the door client money goes through still refuses a firm-funds line outright and was not relaxed to make room; the cushion carries the same `account_balance` zero floor a matter ledger carries, which is how "a bank charge is never borne by client funds" becomes a database guarantee rather than a comparison somebody could forget; a distinct `trust:firmFunds` capability seeded to Owner/Admin alone gates opening and funding it, narrower than the authority to release a client's money; and opening it is refused outright on a pooled interest-bearing account, which the researched rules exempt from the charges the cushion would pay. The three-way proof gained a fourth figure: the cushion is its own leg, never folded into the client total (which previously summed every node and would have counted firm money as client money) and never left out of the comparison (which would have reported a `book-to-client` disagreement on every account that enabled it, poisoning the one signal that means something bypassed the composition guard). Three fitness queries re-prove all of it over stored rows. Three questions are flagged for the owner, all places the rule text is silent: whether the cushion carries a maximum, whether surplus firm funds may be withdrawn, and whether the pooled-account refusal is too strict.

**Unclaimed client funds** (owner flag T16) ship as a read and an evidence trail, and deliberately not as an escheat feature: the primary-source research found designated client trust accounts exempt from Nevada's unclaimed-property presumption outright, with the one onward destination the rules name being permissive rather than compelled, so there is no deadline to count down to and no screen says otherwise. Dormancy is a comparison made at read time against a window **the reader states** — no stored flag, no sweep, no default period — mirroring the calendar's overdue posture and for the same reason: a firm may have been in contact with the client this morning in a way the platform never saw. The read reports the earliest receipt still on the ledger separately from the last activity, because the rules' clocks run from receipt of the property. Each locate attempt is recorded when it is made, with the address or number actually used, in an append-only file that carries one open review per client ledger. **Every money movement takes a person, and the gate is the absence of the inputs**: closing a review as a distribution names a disbursement that already posted through the ordinary authorized path, and the closing composer receives no amount, payee, date, or method, so there is nothing it could assemble into a ledger entry — it writes one row and moves nothing. The remittance packet, the jurisdiction type-fit repair, the separate non-trust holder regime, and the routes and interface are written into the slice's spec rather than half-built.
`@magna-carta/costs` + `@magna-carta/billing-core` (shared WIP lifecycle); first per-firm queue consumer; recoverable-charge seam. cost→A/R + LEDES → 3·4.
