The trust kind composes **no ledger entry** — the transfer's operating leg already credited the receivable — with a dedicated test proving the subledger still equals the control account after a trust-funded fee, and a fitness query re-proving exactly one receivable credit per trust application over stored rows. Over HTTP as `POST /api/v1/billing/trust-applications` on `billing:apply`, idempotency required. The trust-refusal-to-problem mapping moved to one shared home now that two route modules reach it.

**All four fee models — the owner's docket direction, built.** `matter_billing_arrangement` is the per-matter fee agreement, versioned append-only in the rate-engine shape hardened by trigger: a fee change is a NEW version, versions are dense per matter, exactly one is in force, and the only edit a version ever takes is the one-time close of its `valid_to` — because invoice lines now record the agreement version that composed them (`invoice_line.billing_arrangement_id`), so what a finalized bill was computed under is permanent. Absence means hourly. The flat fee is one line plus zero-amount claims on the contributing time (instalments representable, over-billing reported by fitness query); a flat-fee or contingency matter refuses hourly time claims by name while its costs stay claimable. The contingency fee is ALWAYS DERIVED, never stored: `matter_recovery` records the settlement or judgment (void-with-reason its only edit) and the fee is computed at composition — the agreed share against the gross recovery or the recovery net of advanced hard costs, per the recorded election — landing as an ordinary reviewable line. The evergreen retainer records target and floor on the agreement, reads trust's own AVAILABLE figure, and records a `retainer_replenishment_request` (observed balance, shortfall, one open per matter, resolution-only edits) emitting `billing.retainer.replenishment_requested` — the notifications seam, with the below-floor automation belonging to 3·7. NO new trust write shape anywhere: advance fees sit where the agreement's recorded destination says, and money leaves trust only through the existing earned-fee application. Per owner override B4, the multi-matter render shape is a fact on the invoice model: a firm default (per-matter pages plus a summary ships as the default), overridable per finalize, snapshot onto `invoice.render_shape` with the letterhead, and served by a render-model derivation the PDF tail will consume. Migration idx 49 (`20260807T060000_billing-fee-models`); thirteen new chokepoint routes on the existing six billing permissions.

**Corrections after finalization — the last named gap in the spine.** A finalized bill is frozen by trigger, so every correction is a SECOND permanent record: `credit_note` and `credit_note_line` are append-only from birth and refused against anything but a finalized invoice, and the invoice's own total never moves — a note lands as an application against `applied_minor`. What a note cannot absorb opens a `client_credit`, whose "open" is DERIVED from a frozen `amount_minor` and a delta-updated `discharged_minor` under a bounds CHECK rather than a status column; the one exit that moves no money (setting it against a later bill of the same client, any of their matters) is built, and refund-from-operating and return-to-trust are named and deliberately not performed. A write-off posts bad debt to its own account and cannot exceed the unpaid balance. A reversal unwinds an application and its posting and refuses two kinds by name: a trust transfer (putting client money back is a trust movement, composed and authorized there) and a credit note (a permanent document is answered by a further correction). The application row now records WHICH posting it rode with, held by trigger — none for a trust transfer, none for a credit note (one posting per note, across however many per-matter applications, including none when the bill is already paid), exactly one for every other kind — which makes the no-double-credit rule a database guarantee for the first time and lets a new fitness query prove the mirror condition. A matter does not close over an open client credit (hard block, proven twice, no override); it deliberately does not block on an unpaid receivable, whose lawful exit is a write-off.

**And the contingency shrunk-basis residual the fee-models review left open.** The over-billing report compared the GROSS finalized fee lines, and a finalized line cannot be edited — so the credit note that resolves a shrunk basis had no effect on the report demanding it, and the matter stayed flagged forever with the correct remedy already applied. A credit-note line may now name the invoice line it credits, and both the composer's offset and `contingencyBilledBeyondEntitlementStatement` read billed net of attributed credits. `readContingencyResidual` states the residual as an amount and names the finalized fee lines a correction would be aimed at with what each bill still owes — and issues nothing, because what a firm owes back after a settlement collapses is a decision with a client in it. Migration idx 56 (`20260813T010000_billing-credit-notes`); seven new chokepoint routes on the existing billing keys, so no permission inventory moved. **Credit notes carry no number — whether one draws from the invoice sequence, its own, or none is an open owner question.**

**The delivery record — "has this bill been given to the client" becomes answerable.** `invoice_delivery` is one append-only row per attempt (channel, recipient reference, the firm-supplied delivery date, external reference, outcome, and who recorded it), which is why "sent" is deliberately not an invoice status: a bill goes out possibly several times by several channels, and modelling that as a status would force the finalized row to stay mutable for its least load-bearing field. A second delivery is a second row and nothing is ever edited or withdrawn — three triggers hold that unconditionally, including the BEFORE INSERT guard that catches `INSERT OR REPLACE`, which fires neither of the other two. Two more triggers hold what the row can describe: a delivery names a FINALIZED bill (a draft is still being written; a voided draft was never issued) and cannot predate the bill's own issue date, which is the one thing about a firm-supplied date the platform can check.

**It is a record, not a transmission, and that is the design rather than a shortfall.** Nothing renders an invoice and nothing carries one to a client, so every row is a delivery the FIRM made and is reporting — handed over at a meeting, posted, emailed from the firm's own mailbox, submitted to the client's e-billing portal. A table that could only hold deliveries the platform performed would leave every out-of-band delivery unrecordable, which is the firm that most needs to answer the question. The record is SURFACED, never a gate: `readInvoiceDeliveryState` rides `readInvoiceDetail` so the surface that decides to take fees from a client's trust ledger cannot forget to show it, and finalization alone still gates — a hard delivery gate would be satisfied by firms recording deliveries that never happened. The state read distinguishes a bill never sent from a bill chased and not landed (attempt counts beside the flag), and reports the FIRST recorded success rather than the latest, because when the client was first given the bill is the question a jurisdiction asks. A batched form answers a whole set of open receivables in one query rather than N+1. `billing.invoice.delivered` is emitted carrying identifiers, the channel and the outcome — never the recipient reference, which is the client's own fact and resolves behind the deep link. Migration idx 68 (`20260817T000000_billing-invoice-delivery`); two new chokepoint routes on the existing `billing:draft` and `billing:read` keys, so no permission inventory moved.

Taxes remain open, as do the invoice renderer and LEDES (4) and settlement disbursement statements (a later financial slice). **Two owner questions the delivery record raised and did not answer: whether a delivery recorded in error may be superseded by a correcting row, since the table is append-only and the design names no correction shape; and the `outcome` vocabulary, which the design names as a column without enumerating, built as `delivered`/`failed` — the floor rather than an answered set.**

slices.next: Owner answers on the sixteen flagged questions — the gating ones are G1 (does a starter chart ship), G3 (is period close in scope for this slice), G10/G11 (the two extractions out of shipped billing and reporting code), and G15 (do these books ship ahead of payments' manual receipt); then sub-slice 3·5·1, the chart of accounts, which also gives billing the role-mapping surface it currently has none of
slices.notes:
**Designed — the operating books as a classification laid over the one ledger, not a second ledger.** Four additive columns on `ledger_account` (a code, a statement section, a system-account marker, a description), the `type` CHECK untouched and normal balance still derived in its one home, one posting primitive, and a source scan asserting the new package composes no entry, line, or balance write of its own. A firm's operating books and its trust books are provably the same rows, so a bar-audit pack and a balance sheet cannot disagree about what happened. **Supersedes the design and plan on the dormant `slice-3-5-operating-general-ledger` branch**, whose two load-bearing choices were right in July and are wrong now: it assumed this slice would land before billing and invented a `semantic_key` resolver, and billing landed first with `firm_account_role`.

**Trust and operating stay separate structurally, and the new risk is the general journal.** A person typing debits and credits is a third door onto a primitive that is account-agnostic by design, so a journal entry naming a matter leaf and an income account would be balanced, leaf-only, single-currency, correctly dated, and would post client money into fee income. The journal is therefore made incapable of naming a trust account rather than taught the trust rules: every line resolves through **trust's own** `loadTrustAccountRoles` and the whole entry refuses by name unless every line is outside trust — the inverse of a rule trust owns, computed from trust's resolver, so a new tier of trust account is refused the day it exists with no edit here. A fitness query re-proves it over stored rows and catches what no pre-check can: an ordinary account journalled against and later registered as a trust bank leaf. The same refusal binds the vendor-bill and bill-payment composers. Nothing is a flag on `assertTrustComposition` and nothing widens the bank-charge carve-out. A chart **may and must** classify a trust account for statement presentation (a trust bank is an asset, the client-trust liability an equal one, and omitting them hides the relationship an examiner checks) and **may not** map one to an account role, re-section one, or re-type one — with no `is_trust` flag anywhere, because registration is already stored in three places and a fourth could go stale in the one direction that matters.

**Pin 4 resolves in the direction the build order took.** `firm_account_role` is the resolver; a `semantic_key` column is refused because two independently editable maps from meaning to account both look correct in their own surface and one of them is where the money went. The map moves into a pure leaf both consumers can depend on (the `billing-core` precedent, no-behaviour-change gate), exactly two roles are added — `accounts_payable` and `owners_equity`, with deliberately no default expense account — and three configuration guards land, the load-bearing one being that a role's account `type` must match its declared normal balance, since mapping `fee_income` to an asset account inverts every future invoice posting while the entry still balances and the batch still commits.

**Two schema corrections to the prior plan.** Widening `cost_entry.source` is unbuildable (SQLite cannot widen a CHECK without a destructive rebuild of a table holding data), so the bill-to-cost link lives on `vendor_bill_line.disbursement_entry_id` and provenance is derived from it, leaving `cost_entry` untouched. And `vendor_bill.status` becomes a derived state — an append-only payment table plus a bounds-checked `paid_minor` delta, the `invoice_matter_balance` arrangement — so two payments racing for one remainder abort rather than overpay.

**Period close is proposed as a scope addition, with the race closed rather than accepted.** A monotonic lock date in its own table, checked inside `postEntry` because a lock only one caller honours is not a lock and because period membership is a property of the ledger's own `effective_date` column. A reversal always passes, dated into the open period, or fixing a closed month would require reopening it. The close-versus-posting race uses billing's refuse-on-frozen-work pattern: the batch aims a value the lock column's date CHECK forbids at the row only when the lock has moved since the read, so a stale read aborts its own whole batch. Retained earnings is computed, never posted.

**Four statement primitives that refuse rather than degrade**, bitemporal in the shape 3·6 shipped, with the temporal contract moved down into a shared leaf so one validation of a triple exists. A trial balance that does not foot, a balance sheet that does not balance, trust sections that do not net to zero, and any posting account no section would place each refuse by name. Re-sectioning is bounded so it can only move an account within one statement. Nothing is materialised, and the `ledger_line.effective_date` denormalization is argued from this slice's own measurement or not at all. **QuickBooks is a sync structurally**: the `accounting` category declares export operations only with a fitness assertion rejecting any import-shaped operation name, there is no column anywhere that could hold a remote figure, an export refusal is a dispatch outcome, and a divergence caused by editing the remote is stated as undetectable rather than simulated — because detecting it needs the read-back that would make the remote authoritative.

**Five sub-slices, each shippable alone; seven ADR fragments; sixteen questions flagged.** 3·5·1 (the chart) is first because it also closes a live gap — billing refuses to finalize an invoice whose roles are unmapped and there is no surface to map them. **Three things are scoped out rather than half-built**: cash does not arrive until payments' first slice lands, so the operating bank balance moves only through a typed journal entry and the books are correct but sparse; there is no operating bank reconciliation until an importer and the payments clearing account exist; and per-office or per-matter income statements are not designed, because the dimension columns land here and the paths producing income belong to slices this one does not own.

slices.next: Owner answers on the nine flagged questions and on the two defaults this build shipped behind seams; then the filed pack artifact (needs a renderer), then sub-slice 3·6·2 — the financial reports
slices.notes:
**Designed — all four report families, bar-audit pack first, per the owner's scope answer.** A projection layer rather than a subsystem: every quantity is either owned by another package and called rather than reimplemented, a decomposition shipping with a fitness test that proves it sums to its aggregate, or a count or ratio that touches no money the ledger has an opinion about. Nothing recomputes the three-way reconciliation — a closed period prints its frozen attestation verbatim and, where the live proof now differs, both appear labelled. Reproducibility is bitemporal on columns that already exist: an effective-date period plus a `recorded_at` knowledge instant, both on append-only tables, so a stated triple is a pure function of rows that cannot change. Read-only is four checkable mechanisms — a purity fitness scan, GET-only routes, a `reports:*` namespace that grants no write, and the one write (the filed pack artifact and its append-only production record) composed by the route and the queue consumer rather than by the package. Nothing is materialised. Three gaps are named rather than approximated: work in progress, productivity, and realization's standard-value leg are live-only because the work-in-progress stores are mutable and carry no `billed_at`/`voided_at`; profitability is not computable at all for want of a timekeeper cost rate; and a firm-wide operating position waits on slice 3·5's chart of accounts, which is not on `main`. Six ADR fragments. **Nine questions are flagged for the owner** — the load-bearing one being what an ethical wall does to a firm-wide financial total; the trust-compliance pack is settled either way and is never screened, and every response carries a completeness declaration so the later answer costs a field's value rather than a redesign.

**Sub-slice 3·6·1 built — the bar-audit pack, backend only.** `@magna-carta/reporting` lands with the temporal contract (a civil-date period on the effective axis plus a `recorded_at` knowledge instant, validated together, with a live mode that is stamped and says it does not reproduce), the completeness declaration every response carries, and the pack itself: cover, reconciliations, per-client and per-matter ledgers, the receipts-and-disbursements journal, the firm's own bank-charge cushion, exceptions, provenance. Five bitemporal select builders land in the trust package — the settled as-of statements are untouched, because the three-way proof's contract does not move for a report — and a reconciliation closed after the knowledge instant reads as open with no attestation, because printing one would be printing knowledge from after the moment the document claims to be taken at. `GET /api/v1/reports/trust-compliance/{trustAccountId}` serves it on the first of five `reports:` capabilities, all seeded to Owner/Admin alone.

**Read-only is proved at two layers**: a purity scan over the reporting package's own sources rejects a write statement, effect-batch machinery, a domain composer import, or an aggregate of its own over the ledger, and asserts it has sources to check; the conformance suite rejects any mutating route gated on a `reports:` read key. Nothing is materialised, and every decomposition ships with an agreement test proving it sums to the aggregate its owner produces over rows written by the real composers.

**One design correction, recorded as its own decision fragment.** The design asks for the live three-way proof "at the pack's knowledge instant". That is not obtainable: the proof is owned by the trust package and takes no knowledge instant, and writing a bounded copy here would be a second implementation of the reconciliation a firm attested to. The pack calls the owner's function, groups it with the exceptions whose owning reads have the same property, stamps both blocks with their own instant and `boundedByKnowledgeInstant: false`, and says on its face which part of the document may differ between two runs. The reproducibility test strips exactly those two blocks — the first version of it found the exceptions section silently unbounded.

**Measured over the trust volume** at one month and at twelve: client-ledger read 0.6 → 1.4 ms, journal 0.6 → 1.7 ms, whole document 63 → 106 ms, nothing scanning. The cost centre is the per-reconciliation three-way proof rather than the per-row reads, so the `ledger_line.effective_date` denormalization the design held in reserve is not warranted.

**Unbuilt and named:** the filed pack artifact and its production record, which need a renderer this repository cannot run (the conversion engines are not deployed) — the two append-only tables are deliberately out of the migration rather than shipped for nothing to write. Sub-slices 2 to 5 and every screen are untouched. **Two defaults shipped behind named seams and flagged**: zero-balance ledgers are listed, authorizers are named, and a jurisdiction with no reviewed corpus states its refusal on the cover rather than refusing the whole document — which matters today, because every encoded jurisdiction ships unreviewed.

slices.next: Owner flags M1, M2 and M3 — they decide whether a schedule may finalize, whether reminders ship on or off, and whether a payment plan may charge anything
slices.notes: **Design and plan written; the build waits on three owner flags.** The scheduled no-client-present layer over 3·4 — recurring and batch bills, payment reminders, payment plans, and evergreen below-floor replenishment — riding the per-firm cron fan-out and the transactional outbox, with Notifications as the only delivery path. Three absences found during the design reshaped it: there is **no channel to a client** (every notification audience resolves to a member and the portal is not started), there is **no `invoice_delivery` record and no invoice renderer** (the table the billing design specified was never built, though its identifier prefix is registered), and **a cron pass has no actor** — `resolveTrustAuthorizationDisposition` takes a `UserId` and the seeded posture routes a non-holder to a holder, so nothing scheduled can take an earned fee, held by a source scan rather than by discipline. So a reminder is a prompt to the firm rather than a letter to the client, a payment plan is a record and a derived standing rather than a charge, and every automation is tiered by consequence: a draft and a record are free, finalizing and telling a client sit behind a firm setting defaulting off and a still-standing human authorization, and money moving is unreachable. Each automation converges on a UNIQUE index in **billing's own tables** rather than on the notification dedupe key, because the retention sweep deletes the row that key lives on and a once-per-invoice reminder would re-raise the day it aged out. Every run writes one row per target including the skips, with a closed outcome label and never a sentence — and a run row records a decision about the world, never a failure to read it, or one bad afternoon becomes a permanent skip. Thirteen owner flags (series `M`), each with a recommendation.

slices.next: Deepening slices 1-4 built (reporting posture; event triggers + the re-check ledger + the consumers, cron backstop and notification; typed traversal budgets + the closure cap and its truncation record + the batched matcher; matching depth — the two organization match keys, the empty nickname catalogue, and name-role breadth as a firm setting). Slice 5 follows: the adjudication read models and the conflicts report artifact, whose tasks embed owner flags F4 and F5. The firm-marked non-expandable entity (F9) is still unbuilt — slice 3 left it to whichever slice owns the Directory write path and slice 4 deliberately did not take it, since the mark is a traversal control rather than a matching one
slices.notes: No-scorer evidence-tier engine; typed source registry + firm floor; three append-only log tables. Firm personnel resolved as a source, not a Directory node type. Deepening slice 1 adds the reporting posture: one derived per-matter read, an honest zero-hit report, and a vocabulary fitness function — the platform reports what it searched and never concludes. Slice 2 makes the check fire when the corpus moves: one outbox row on each producing write path, the `conflicts_recheck_request` ledger (partial unique index on the open rows, immutable cause, one-way satisfaction, never deleted), separate request and run consumers, a cron drain plus a scheduled re-scan, and `conflicts.hit.surfaced` carrying counts only. The automated path cannot dispose of anything, and two source scans prove it. Slice 3 makes the graph half of search depth real: traversal is budgeted per edge class rather than by one integer (corporate family transitive at no hop cost; control, family and representation one hop each by default), bounded by a per-run closure cap, and both are firm settings recorded verbatim on the check row. Reaching the cap stops the walk and the check records that it was TRUNCATED with the frontier it did not reach — a truncated expansion is never reported as a completed one, the depth analogue of `unavailable` never reading as searched and clean. Degree-based hub suppression is refused and the refusal is held by a test; expired edges are traversed with the expiry on the path step. The N+1 goes in the same change: one subject-facts read per node table over the closure, one batched edge read per traversal round, each blocking channel once over the closure — gated by an equivalence test proving the batched matcher returns exactly the per-entity matcher's hit set over a real corpus. A follow-on pass adds the SECOND bound the traversal slice's measurement asked for: a corpus sweep with the closure pinned shows candidates rising linearly with the Directory (about six tenths of the organization corpus per organization subject, a tenth of the person corpus per person subject, ~99% of it trigram overlap with no other signal), so `candidateCap` now bounds what a run WRITES beside the cap on how far it walks — strongest evidence kept, a co-party surfacing never refused, the refusal recorded per evidence tier and stated in the report, and the bound applied outside both matchers so the equivalence proof stays a proof about the whole answer. Slice 4 closes the ORGANIZATION half of matching depth: two derived keys beside the frozen normalization (`normalized_match_key` at tier 2 for one name spelled two ways, `normalized_match_key_bare` at tier 3 for the same name under a different legal form), and the nickname catalogue shipped empty so every check records the dimension as one it could not search. The keys are computed inside `insertNameStatement` so none of the eight name-writing paths can omit them, filled for existing corpora by a resumable budgeted sweep on the daily cron with no stored cursor, and audited by a fitness probe. The PERSON half — Beider-Morse for cross-origin surnames — was built and then removed on measurement: the only maintained pure-TypeScript encoder (MIT, zero runtime dependencies, so golden rule 14 never applied) compiles its rule tables in 20,377 ms inside workerd against 16 ms in Node, which is past the Workers CPU limit on both the write and the read path, and a lazy dynamic import is worse because Workers forbid runtime module loading. The recall it would buy is measured and recorded (seven cross-origin pairs in thirty that Double Metaphone structurally cannot reach), and the follow-on carries that number as its flip condition. The design's claim that the encoder was additive rows on `directory_name_phonetic_code` is also false and is corrected in the schema: that table's primary key is (name_id, scheme), so it holds one code per name per scheme and cannot hold a variable set. Name-role breadth becomes an explicit firm setting recorded verbatim on the check row beside the name keys compared and the phonetic schemes that ran, shipping the design's recommended default (current, former, maiden, alias) so a married-name change is found at the default band and answering owner flag F1 is a settings edit rather than a release. The load-profile smoke test asserts each new channel actually found something against the real corpus, because a channel that finds nothing reads as coverage and is worse than no channel at all.

slices.next: The two sweeps the load profile found planning through the wrong index (overdue check-out at 15.3ms over 32,723 movements to answer 91, and reviews-due), then receipts (blocked on a matter-routed assembly path), portal visibility (blocked on the portal grant model), the succession/transfer manifest, and the death-date seam the will-deposit catalog computes against (no packet column records a death today)
slices.notes:
Slice 4·2·1 (the register) built: eleven per-firm tables, trigger-enforced append-only movement ledger, mandatory Directory ownership, allocation-ledger custody numbers, holds, and scan binding via a system holding matter. Slice 4·2·2 built the review-and-reporting half: review dates with an anniversary-anchored roll forward and a `reviewed` ledger entry, one query-shaped reminder emission point covering both reviews and overdue check-outs, three register reports (holdings per owner, occupancy per location, holds in force), and printable Code 128 label sheets — twenty-five routes in total. Slice 4·2·3 built gated release: a `released` movement must name who collected the property and carry the authority it leaves on, how the collector was identified, and the member who made that check, frozen on the append-only ledger row and enforced by three `BEFORE INSERT` triggers rather than by a CHECK, so releases recorded before the gate existed stay exactly as they were recorded. Two-signatory release is a per-firm policy, off by default, and the two signatories must be two people. The authority vocabulary is deliberately not invented — the basis is free text a firm writes. Receipts and portal visibility, the other half of 4·2·3, are not built: the document-assembly path is matter-routed and matter-permissioned, and no portal grant model exists. Slice 4·2·4's stocktake half is built: a firm can open a count over the whole register or one branch of the container tree, record observations in batches (a packet seen at a location, a packet looked for and not found, an object on the shelf with no register row), and close it producing a reconciliation of missing, misplaced, unexpected, and unregistered against what the register expected. **A stocktake observes and reports only** — nothing on the path writes the movement ledger, a packet, or an item; corrective movements are named as proposals a person records through the one movement write path, a missing original proposes nothing at all, and a source-scan fitness function holds that boundary. Sighting rows are append-only at the database with the movement ledger's three triggers plus a fourth refusing an observation against a closed count; closing freezes the findings so a reported number cannot drift, and an unfinished count is abandoned rather than closed. Seven routes over the existing two custody permissions, two per-firm tables, no new movement kind. The destruction workflow is built, now that the owner has ratified the shape flags. Raising a request, approving it, and recording that it was carried out are three calls made by at least two people: **the requester and the approver differ by construction**, enforced by database triggers as well as by the service — including the case a column check cannot see, where a request names no requester and any approver would otherwise satisfy it. A decided request is terminal and is re-raised rather than re-decided. Execution appends its `destroyed` entry through the one movement write path, so a destruction carries a person's name on the same append-only ledger as everything else, and the request row names the ledger entry it produced. **Two refusals carry no override anywhere:** a hold in force stops both the request and the execution (asked twice, because a hold placed between them is exactly what a hold is for), and an item recorded as an irreplaceable original is never destructible — that refusal now binds the ordinary movement path and the database itself, not only the workflow, so it holds for a write path nobody has written. No retention period, default, derived date, or sweep exists anywhere on the path. Five columns and nine triggers on the existing table; no new permission.

The will-deposit duty catalog is built with **Nevada as the first encoded jurisdiction**, following the trust-rules posture: an unencoded jurisdiction is REFUSED rather than answered, "not recorded" stays a different refusal from "not encoded", and there is no baseline. Nevada carries the NRS 136.050(1) 30-day delivery duty quoted verbatim with its citation, the clock starting at knowledge of the death, both delivery targets, the subsection 3 civil liability, and the public-record consequence of delivering to the clerk; the personal representative's own duty and the NRS 136.060 court-ordered production sit beside it, the latter carrying no interval because the court names the time. The verified absence of any lifetime court deposit is encoded as an explicit negative. County lodging (EDCR 4.40, Second Judicial District Rule 57.7) is keyed BELOW the state, and Nevada's other nine districts refuse on their own terms. The catalog carries what the statute says and never an interpretation: the research's open questions — constructive knowledge, "reasonable cause" case law — stay open, and a due date is computed only from a date a person recorded. **No packet column records a death**, so that computation ships as a seam. Deliberately not built and still owner decisions: the NRS 133 qualified-custodian role, the clerk-versus-personal-representative guidance surface, and the succession/transfer manifest.

The remaining ratified flags are wired: the location depth cap of eight is proven at eight and at nine on both write paths (C4), the ownership label on an owner link is validated against the firm's own catalog when it has configured one and against nothing when it has not (C5), and the matter close path gained an advisory-only notice — closing a matter surfaces the custody packets linked to it, reports a count and nothing identifying, and never blocks (C6), which is deliberately a separate mechanism from the close-precondition hook rather than a precondition with a softer flag.

slices.notes:
Slice 4·3·1 built: the register core, on the design's recommended defaults for every owner flag. **Eight per-firm tables** — the asset row anchored `NOT NULL` to one matter, the per-firm type catalog under a closed ten-value platform class, the real-property and financial-account attribute tables, the append-only valuation history, interests, the document link, and the sealed identifier — plus two permissions, thirteen seeded catalog entries, the firm's starting interest-label list, and **seventeen routes**. An asset row is **one matter's assertion**: there is deliberately no cross-matter thing identity, because the same house in a divorce and in an estate has different dates, values, encumbrances, and privilege, and a shared row would have to reconcile them. **Two fields make a row** (a class and a description) — the deliberate inversion of Custodian's mandatory owner link, because here the catastrophe is a register nobody fills in — and a valuation and the class attributes ride the create call, with a bounded bulk route in the first slice rather than deferred. **A valuation is appended, never updated and never deleted, and no current-value column exists on any table**: enforced by the custody ledger's three `RAISE(ABORT)` triggers (update, delete, and the replace guard that catches an `INSERT OR REPLACE`), by a source scan over the package, and by a `PRAGMA`-walking test that no asset table carries an undated value column. A correction is a compensating row naming the row it corrects, which supersedes it in every read while both stay on the record. The **as-of read returns amount, date, and basis as one object** so a value cannot be rendered without the date it speaks to, and **a date before an asset's first valuation resolves to nothing** rather than to the earliest figure — proven as a table, alongside exactly-on, between-two, and corrected-row-never-resolves. **The class is frozen at creation** and the patch schema accepts the field so a caller naming it gets an explainable refusal rather than a silent strip. **Documents are many-to-many** and deliberately diverge from `custody_scan`'s unique file index — one brokerage statement lists four accounts — and no byte reaches an asset route: the File Manager's presigned-upload and quarantine chokepoint is the only ingest, and a file filed under another matter is refused. **Identifiers split by what they are**: a parcel number is public record and stays a plaintext searchable column, while a full account, policy, certificate, or tax number is a registered protected column reachable only through the existing `readProtected` chokepoint — permission-gated, audited before any plaintext, with every list, detail, and report projecting the four-character suffix on a row shape that carries no field a full value could ride on, and a named refusal rather than a blank when the decrypt permission is absent. **No credential is storable anywhere**: a password, passphrase, seed or recovery phrase, private key, personal identification number, or safe combination is refused BY NAME before anything is sealed, with its own problem type whose message names the custody register as the correct home. The class registry carries the firearm handling notice now, standing and non-jurisdictional, guarded by a test asserting it names no jurisdiction, cites no statute, and carries no numeral; nothing branches on it.

Deliberately not built and named as seams: the six remaining attribute tables and their classes (declared in the registry and refused by name with "arrives in 4·3·2"), encumbrances and net equity (`matter_asset_valuation.encumbrance_id` lands now because adding it later means rebuilding a table whose triggers have to be dropped to do it), the grouped estate schedule, the custody item link coming into use, the asset merge subjects and the one new assembly source, the firm's own fields on an asset, carry-forward from a prior matter, the parcel and valuation integration adapters, and portal visibility. The load-profile asset corpus and the as-of schedule measurement are the next thing after 4·3·2.

Slices 4·3·2 and 4·3·3 built (reconciled against the plan: the protected identifier and the firearm handling notice landed EARLY in 4·3·1, so 4·3·2's remainder was the attribute tables, encumbrances, and the schedule). **Seven new per-firm tables** — the six remaining one-to-one attribute tables and `matter_asset_encumbrance` — plus one additive index on the valuation history and twenty-six seeded catalog entries, taking the register to **every one of its ten classes**. The line between a public-record identifier and a credential-adjacent secret now has its sharpest cases on both sides: a vehicle identification number, a plate, and a firearm serial are plaintext and indexed because searching by them is the point, while `matter_asset_digital_asset` has **no column a credential could ride on at all** and the write path refuses one by name. A firearm's `regulated_category` is free text a person asserted and is read by nothing — no code classifies an item, determines a recipient, or produces a deadline. **An encumbrance's balance is a valuation row naming it**, so one append-only table, one trigger set, one as-of query shape, and net equity as one read with a sign flip — and the write path refuses a balance naming a charge on a different asset, because that makes the equity of two assets wrong with neither looking wrong. **Equity is computed and never stored, and withheld rather than approximated**: an unrecorded balance makes it unavailable rather than nil (which would overstate exactly the assets a firm must be careful about) and a mixed-currency pair nets to nothing at all; negative equity is reported as negative, because a house worth less than its mortgage is the ordinary condition of many estates. **The schedule** groups by class as of a required, never-defaulted date, subtotals per class per currency, states the unvalued count rather than hiding it, keeps `undetermined` as its own group, and withholds a group's equity subtotal when one balance in it is unstated — five batched reads for a whole matter, never one per asset. **The custody link comes into use**: set and cleared through the patch route against an item the write path proves exists, with the asset detail composing location, status, and hold state by READING Custodian at request time and storing none of it; a source scan in both directions holds the boundary, refusing any mention of `declared_value_*` in the package and any write into a custody table. **Eleven merge subjects on ONE new source**, collection-only by construction: no `assetClass` subject declares a scalar (an estate with two houses would make every scalar an absence naming the count), `value` and `valueAsOf` are declared and set together or not at all, `accountSuffix` is the facet and the full number has no key, and a manifest naming all eleven issues exactly the one read a manifest naming one issues — the a-subject-costs-nothing property, holding on the first outside subsystem to join the catalogue.

**The firm's own fields on an asset — the last buildable half of 4·3·3 — is now built, and it took no migration.** The plan asked for "one additive migration, coordinated with the Custodian `custodyPacket` widening so both values land in one"; the schema says otherwise and the plan is deviated from deliberately. `custom_field.target` has been a bare `text NOT NULL` with **no CHECK** since the per-firm baseline, and drizzle's `enum` option is a TypeScript narrowing that emits no SQL and is not even recorded in the lineage snapshots — so after the widening `check-snapshots` reports the per-firm head already current and `generate` has nothing to emit. Shipping an empty migration would have added a file every firm must apply, doing nothing, implying a constraint that does not exist. With no migration there is also nothing for the two widenings to share, so `custodyPacket` is left to the Custodian stream rather than added here: putting in a target no reader recognises is exactly the failure this change is about, and the request schema's refusal of it is now asserted by a test.

**What the absent CHECK means is that the readers carry the whole of the safety**, so the vocabulary stopped being written out in three places. `CUSTOM_FIELD_TARGETS` in `packages/custom-fields/src/types.ts` is the one home; the define-field request schema derives its `z.enum` from it, the scoped read takes its parameter type from it, and a fitness test pins the drizzle column's `enumValues` to it — the one restatement the dependency direction forces (a schema package cannot import a domain package that imports it) cannot drift. Every reader was walked. The engine's value path needed nothing: `setCustomFieldValue` validates against the FIELD's definition and `target_row_id` has never referenced a table on any axis, so the value-integrity rules hold on the third axis unchanged. **The merge catalogue's `target = 'matter'` filter is kept** — a `custom.<handle>` key is a scalar resolved against the one row an assembly has, and an asset field's answers live on one of a matter's many asset rows, so admitting one would mint a key that binds at registration and resolves to an absence on every document forever. That filter is now covered by a test written over the whole target vocabulary, so a fourth axis arrives excluded from documents and has to be argued in. Scoping is per class through the engine's existing `attachment_id`, and the asset detail composes it at the route in one read whatever the field count — `@magna-carta/matter-assets` depends on no other domain package and does not start now.

**The starter schedule template is NOT built, and the blocker is a missing mechanism rather than missing content.** Nothing on `main` distributes a template the platform authored: no template package, no committed `.docx` outside a LibreOffice conversion fixture, no `document_template` seed in either lineage, no template role, no adopt route, no `source_form_key` column. The document-automation design left cross-firm template distribution open, to settle "before the first real client"; the Nevada court-form library design then answered it — reference data in a pure package that a firm **adopts** through the ordinary registration pipeline, with provenance columns and supersede-not-replace — and that build is gated on owner flags N1 through N5, none answered. A bespoke second path for one schedule would pre-empt that answer and leave two ways a firm receives platform content. The register's half is complete (eleven subjects with `itemFields`, one batched source, the repeating-block vocabulary), so a firm-authored upload works today. Two owner questions are on the ledger node `matter-assets.schedule-template`: whether non-court starter content waits on N1–N5, and what an estate schedule should actually say — heading, grouping, columns, whether unvalued assets are listed or counted — which neither the design nor ADR-0255's A-flags specify and which every firm provisioned afterwards inherits.

Still not built: a supplied schedule template (above), the load-profile asset corpus and the as-of schedule measurement, carry-forward from a prior matter, the parcel and valuation integration adapters, and portal visibility. A firm's own field on an asset is deliberately not a merge field — that would be a per-item field inside the asset collections, which is a different feature from widening the target.

The first cut of this slice shipped the opposite model — an identity row plus a revision chain, three `RAISE(ABORT)` triggers, and withdrawal as a state — and the owner replaced it hours later: replacing a note with another note every time somebody fixes a word accumulates without end. The reversal is a reviewed rebuild that carries every standing note across with its current text, and it costs what it costs: nothing records what a note said before an edit, and a deletion leaves only an audit row naming no content. slices.notes:
**Sub-slice 5·1·1 built — the Rust discovery core, the sub-slice with the most unknowns and no Cloudflare, database, or worker in it.** `crates/discovery-core` on the engine-host seam: I/O-free, threadless, dual-target (native + `wasm32`), with a seven-code fixed error set whose own test proves no file content can reach an error payload. **Identification reads bytes and cannot read a name** — `identify` has no parameter a file name could arrive through, so a production's wrong names cannot route anything; comparing the two is a separate call whose answer is reported and never acted on, and a spreadsheet renamed to a picture still identifies as a spreadsheet. A ZIP is refined into the package it actually is (word-processing, workbook, presentation, OpenDocument, or a plain archive) and an OLE2 into the document it actually is (legacy Word/Excel/PowerPoint, an Outlook message, or an encrypted package) from entry names alone, with no decompression. **Normalization is the determinism boundary** — line endings, canonical composition, exotic spacing, and invisible characters all settle before anything derived, and everything derived is derived from its output; **the passage chunker moved out of `packages/search/src/extraction.ts` byte-for-byte**, carrying that suite's own corpus with the expected values copied rather than recomputed, because web and desktop feeding one index must agree about what a document says. Committed cross-target vectors run natively and under `wasm-pack`. Native extractors for text (with charset detection), OOXML (including shared-string resolution, so a workbook yields its words and not its indexes), OpenDocument, RTF, email over `crates/email-core`, and **PDF text layers over `crates/pdf-core` — the born-digital PDF that the shipped extraction port records as unextractable now extracts its real text and is never sent to recognition**. Archives enumerate without decompressing and expand under five guards checked before a byte is retained (depth, total bytes, ratio, entry count, and unconditional path-traversal rejection), with an encrypted entry reported rather than failing its siblings and a too-deep nested archive recorded rather than opened. Hosted by `containers/discovery` + `apps/discovery-worker` on the file-repair container pattern: `enableInternet` false, no `r2` feature, an engine failure a 422 carrying only the stable code. **No C-backed feature on any path**, asserted by a test that reads the crate's own manifest, and a hostile-input sweep runs every fixture through truncation, bit-flips, and absurd declared lengths against every entry point. The custodian-vocabulary gate ships early, scoped to the discovery trees, self-testing so it cannot silently stop biting.

**Sub-slice 5·1·2 built — the review-set model, the object every deferred discovery feature is a function over.** `packages/discovery` plus six per-firm tables in one migration (`20260806T080000_discovery-5-1-2`, journal idx 43). **A review document is a pointer and never a copy**: it names a `file_version` or an `email_message` the firm already holds, so the internal lanes move no bytes, re-read none, and reuse the hash computed at ingest and the scan verdict already recorded — and it pins the VERSION, so a file that gains a new version does not silently change a corpus already certified. **The vocabulary is mechanical**: `recordCustodian` / `record_custodian` / "record custodian", two words everywhere, with the shipped gate now biting on this package's own prose; record custodians are review-set-scoped because the same name in two matters is not assertably the same person. **The transcript control is a required field with no default in either direction** — every load declares `transcript_scope`, the column is `NOT NULL` with no default, an omission is refused, and `include` is refused BY NAME until the lane that reaches transcripts exists, because silently dropping it would produce a corpus that does not match its declaration and honouring it in name would produce a manifest claiming a sweep that never happened. **Three state machines are triggers, not conventions**: a review set moves open → locked → closed and a reopen aborts at the database; a load moves declared → loading → processing → complete, fails only before completing, and is reversed only once complete; a document leaves a terminal processing state only by an explicit reset to `pending`, so it can never flip between `processed` and `excepted`. **The reconciliation is a row CHECK** — a load cannot reach `complete` while loaded ≠ processed + excepted. **The ceiling is refused at declaration** with the count and the ceiling in the message. **Discovery is its own permission namespace** (`discovery:read` / `:manageReviewSets` / `:load`), which IS the access rule: a member holding every `matters:*` and `files:*` grant on the matter reaches no review set on it, proven by a route test. The `DiscoveryLoadCoordinator` holds its cursor in durable storage and nothing on the instance, so an eviction mid-fan-out resumes where the load actually got to; email enters as a family; a quarantined version is refused by name rather than skipped.

Settled by the build and recorded: the per-review-set access LIST the design recommended is named for the review surface rather than built (a list nothing renders is a list nothing enforces); the occurrence columns are `primary_review_document_id` + `duplicate_review_document_id`; and the platform-wide widening of the custodian-vocabulary gate that the tool's own comment scheduled for this slice is refused as written and the comment corrected — the shipped Custodian register legitimately owns the bare word as its subsystem name, its package specifier, and its route.

Not built here and named: processing — the queue lane, the composite extraction port, deduplication and occurrences, the exception table and the manifest (5·1·3) — and corpus indexing, the review-document list read, and the load profile (5·1·4). No user-facing surface exists yet, which is why UI is not applicable rather than deferred; the load profile is likewise 5·1·4's, which is why it stays `todo` while the model it measures is built.

**Sub-slice 5·1·3 part-built — the processing lane and the composite extraction port, which is the wire between the two halves that had already shipped.** `DISCOVERY_PROCESS` is its own queue with its own dead-letter queue at concurrency 4, apart from every ingest lane, because a load at the ceiling is a quarter of a million documents and the alternative is a firm's interactive uploads queued behind an opposing party's production. Dispatch is a keyset-paged walk off the load coordinator's durable cursor — resumable across an eviction or a deploy, safe to run twice because it selects only what is still `pending` — and it starts only once allocation is complete, so the reconciliation a load completes against is never counted against a corpus that is still growing. **The extraction port is composite for real now**: the pure-Rust engine reads natively (PDF text layers, OOXML, OpenDocument, RTF, email, plain text — identified from the bytes, never the file name), recognition is asked only about pages the engine reports as pixels, and a 1997 binary office file goes through the consented office container so the CONVERSION can be read by the memory-safe engine — the parser that touches an opposing party's bytes stays pure Rust even for a format no pure-Rust parser exists for, and the identified format on the record stays the legacy one. When the engine service is unbound the shipped in-Worker PDF reader plus recognition still runs, unchanged.

**Every extraction records its ROUTE**, which is the fact the corpus could not previously state and the reason the born-digital-PDF defect was invisible until somebody read the code: `review_document.extraction_route` names the engines in the order they ran, `pages_recognized` counts how many pages are a machine's reading of a picture rather than the author's characters, and the per-page provenance goes to the R2 sidecar. **A disposition and a diagnosis are two fields**: the port keeps its three reasons (park, terminal, retry) because the pipeline does three things, and gains a separate `code` carrying the engine's own stable string, mapped to the closed exception vocabulary by a table proved TOTAL against the port's own export rather than a copy. A refusal code the router does not recognize is treated as transient rather than filed under the nearest name — an unnamed reason means the engine and the worker are at different versions, and inventing a sentence for a report nobody checked is worse than retrying. **A document an undeployed engine has not read is `pending` with `processing_deferred_reason` on the row, not `excepted`**: the two terminal states stay two, and neither of them means "we have not got to it". Bulk stays out of the database — text and sidecar to R2, pointers on the row — and a quarantined version is refused from the version's recorded status without a parser ever being handed the bytes.

**Measured rather than asserted**, at the standard 25,000-document review-set volume on a migrated node-sqlite per-firm database (machine-relative, this box): the mid-walk dispatch page 0.231 ms median / 0.321 ms p95; the whole-load reconciliation tally 3.266 / 3.327; the exception report's counts-by-code 0.157 / 0.186; the parked-document count 0.468 / 0.494; the per-document claim-and-process write pair 0.101 / 0.333. Every volume-shaped read walks an index and the dispatch walk sorts from one — the reconciliation is allowlisted as a whole-load aggregate, which is what it is. **The database after 25,000 review documents and their pointed-at file rows is 44 MiB**, which extrapolates to roughly 440 MiB at the 250,000 ceiling — the arithmetic the ceiling was derived from, now re-derived against a measurement.

Also settled: the conversion registry gains `doc`/`xls`/`ppt` as sources and `xlsx`/`pptx` as targets with office edges onward to PDF, which is what routing a legacy binary through the one home for conversion actually requires and which makes those files convertible in the file-converter tool too; two new object classes for the derived text and sidecar; and a firm with no provisioned bucket parks its dispatch by name rather than failing the load that committed correctly.

Not built here and named: deduplication and occurrence rows, container families over the guarded archive expansion the engine already has, and the manifest and exception report written at load completion — the rest of 5·1·3. The discovery volume in the SHARED load profile is deliberately not added: the corpus is an order of magnitude larger than everything else in a firm's database and folding it into the shared generator would change every other domain's baseline identity for a table none of them read, so the processing measurements seed their own volume on the email-filing precedent and the shared volume lands with the review-document list read in 5·1·4.

**Sub-slice 5·1·3 finished — deduplication with occurrence rows, container families, and the two record artifacts a firm hands to another party.**

**The exception report is the piece the slice was worth doing for.** A production is a claim — _we produced everything we could read_ — and without a document the claim is an assertion. The report names every item the claim excludes and gives the reason for each, from the closed vocabulary in which every code is a different sentence to a court: `encrypted` and `password-protected` stay apart because a password can be asked for and a key cannot, and `no-text-extracted` is on the list precisely so a document that yields nothing is listed rather than indexed as empty. It is written per load in a machine-readable and a printable form, alongside a manifest of what arrived, and **only once the load reconciles** — and reconciliation is checked twice, once against the counters the consumer advanced relatively and once by counting the rows themselves, because a report reconciled against the number it was drawn from would reconcile with anything.

**Both artifacts are REPRODUCIBLE, and that is a property of the generator rather than a habit.** The renderers are pure — no binding, no bucket, no database, and no clock. The knowledge instant is an argument, and it is the load row's `updated_at`: the moment its last counter moved, which is the moment the corpus stopped moving for that load. Nothing advances it afterwards, so a second run reads the same instant and renders the same header; taking `now` would make every rebuild a different document, which is the difference between a record and a snapshot. Every set arrives keyset-ordered by identifier, nothing is derived from the environment, and the keys are derived so a retry overwrites its own object with the same bytes. A test renders twice and compares; a source scan fails the module on a clock. The manifest is streamed into R2 in fixed multipart parts rather than assembled in memory, because a load at the ceiling is a quarter of a million document entries.

**Deduplication decides what a reviewer never sees, so it is built to be inspectable.** The identity is the content hash the ingest gate already recorded, or the email record model's own dedup key for a message — **never the near-duplicate fingerprint on the same row**, which collides by design and would be suppressing a document from review on a heuristic; clustering over it is the review slice's job and it shows documents rather than hiding them. A document with no recorded hash gets no group at all rather than a group of one. Primacy is taken by ONE guarded statement (`WHERE NOT EXISTS` a holder) and held by a partial unique index, so a group can never have two primaries; a copy that finds a holder that has not finished parks and throws, and the queue brings it back one redelivery later because dispatch walks in identifier order. **The duplicate row survives** with its own custodian, its own load and its own terminal state, pointing at the primary's text object rather than a second copy of it, and inheriting the primary's named codes on its own row when the primary is one nothing could read — so the custodian who held an encrypted document is counted as having held one. An occurrence row makes every suppressed copy reachable from the copy a reviewer opens, and "which custodians held this document" is one indexed read.

**A container family is a chain-of-custody claim.** An archive is expanded by the engine under its five existing guards — nothing here second-guesses them — and every entry re-enters the ordinary ingest gate by the same path an email attachment takes: presigned session, magic-byte sniff, content hash, malware scan. There is no discovery bypass and no second way to put bytes in a firm's bucket. Entries are sorted by path before they are numbered, so a re-processing gives the same entry the same family sequence; the archive becomes the family head, `processed` with **no text object** (an empty text object for a container would assert it holds no words, which is the assertion the exception vocabulary exists to avoid) and an entry listing in its sidecar. Entries the engine described rather than opened become one exception per KIND carrying a count and a kind and **never a path** — a path inside an opposing party's production is free text somebody writes a name into. Expansion is one level per document, absolutely and not by counting: the engine already recursed to its own nesting ceiling, so a child that is itself a container is one it declined to open and it says so.

**Found and fixed:** a document waiting on the scan gate parked and was acked, so nothing would ever look again — it now re-reads the row and throws so the queue redelivers, which is what a container's children need since their bytes cross the gate after their message exists. A `quarantined` verdict is deliberately never re-read: the two failure directions are not symmetrical.

Also settled: the extraction facts gain the digest set the engine already computed in the same pass, so MD5 and SHA-1 reach the row (SHA-256 stays the ingest gate's value — two authorities on whether two documents are the same document is one too many), and a legacy binary keeps the digests of the bytes that arrived rather than of the conversion made to read them; the exception row gains its load so the report walks its own index; the lane's message becomes a two-kind union with the absent `kind` still reading as a document, so messages in flight across a deploy still route; and the record artifacts carry a `review-load-record` object class, stamped apart from the derived text and sidecars so a collection rule cannot delete the evidence and keep the cache.

**Three deviations from the design, recorded rather than silently taken:** the manifest carries three digests rather than five (the shipped row has three columns, and no load-file specification asks for SHA-384 or SHA-512); engine VERSION pinning is replaced by the extraction routes the corpus itself observed, because no engine reports a version over its service binding today and inventing one would be worse than omitting it; and an exception row may sit on a document whose terminal state is `processed`, which is what a container with encrypted entries actually is — the report renders the state beside every reason rather than an advisory-code list being invented.

Not built here and named: the review-document index enqueue into the review-set corpus, opt-in semantic indexing, the review-document list read, and the discovery volume in the shared load profile — all 5·1·4. No review surface; the user guide for the exception report is authored ahead of the screens, as the review-set guide already is.

**Sub-slice 5·1·4 built — a review set becomes its own search corpus, and the read every review surface will page through exists and is measured.** The index scope key had been widened from a matter to a corpus everywhere except the half that decides disclosure: the split CATALOG was still keyed by matter, so a review set indexed under its matter would have put material an opposing party produced into the result set of an ordinary matter search — which under a protective order is not a cache miss. `index_split` gains `corpus_kind` and `corpus_id`, every scope read in the catalog moves onto them, and `matter_id` stays as provenance that nothing enumerates by; a suite that deliberately puts both corpora on the SAME matter proves the separation, and fails on every assertion if any read goes back to the matter column. On that, `enqueueReviewDocumentForIndexing` runs through the same coordinator and the same consumer as the version-keyed enqueue. **What differs is only where the passages come from**: a review document's text was already extracted, certified and written to R2, so indexing reads that object rather than handing an opposing party's bytes to a second parser that would give the corpus a second answer about what the document says. The text object gains a form-feed page separator so the pages come back as the passages they were — a form feed cannot occur inside one, because normalization drops every control character before anything is derived — and the pairing with the sidecar's page list is REFUSED rather than guessed when the two disagree, because a search hit that names the wrong page of a production is worse than no hit: somebody cites it. Only the primary of a duplicate group is indexed, which is the whole economic argument for deduplicating.

**A document the index has not taken is recorded on its own row rather than as an exception, and that is a deviation from the plan taken deliberately.** The plan asked for a `review_document_exception` on a `failed` or `deferred` outcome. The exception vocabulary is a CLOSED list held by a CHECK constraint, every code in it is a sentence about what could not be READ, and every one is rendered into a report a firm hands to another party — so "our own search index has not caught up" is not one of them, a later deploy would silently change the number, and widening the list is a rebuild of a shipped table. `review_document.index_state` and `index_deferred_reason` give the property the plan actually wanted: the backlog is countable and pageable from the corpus rather than only from a Durable Object somebody has to know to open. The one index-stage failure that IS about the document — its derived text gone from the bucket — files `source-bytes-missing`, which the vocabulary already has. Whether an unindexed document should additionally be an exception is on the ledger as an owner question.

**The reads.** The review-document list page filtered by Custodian of Record, load, family, processing state and exception code; the live exception surface with its counts by reason; the occurrences a suppressed copy stays reachable through; and what the corpus still owes the index. The list is keyset-paged over `(sort_date, id)` in **two segments rather than one predicate**: a production routinely arrives with documents nothing can date, a descending sort puts those after every dated one, and a single keyset clause over a nullable column either drops the whole undated tail or becomes an OR the planner cannot turn into a range. A test walks the corpus one document at a time across the boundary and asserts nothing repeats and nothing is dropped.

**Found while building on it, and closed: none of the discovery surface was access-scoped except coding.** The review-set LIST was not, and a name is enough — "Plaintiff's production, Ridgeway settlement" on a matter tells a reader a production was received. Neither were the review set, its loads, its Custodians of Record, or any write route: a member holding every discovery permission and on no access list could rename or CLOSE a walled review set, which releases its derived artifacts irreversibly. All of them now go through the list and answer ABSENT rather than refused, and the visibility fitness sweep grew a second registry so the nine new reads are held to the same wall from the same table-driven pass.

**The load profile found a real defect on its first run, which is what it is for.** The list page — the read every reviewer makes hundreds of times a day — cost 10.3 ms per page mid-corpus at the ceiling, because SQLite turns `a < ? OR (a = ? AND b < ?)` into a scan from the end of the index down to the cursor rather than a seek. The same predicate as a row value is **0.26 ms and flat with corpus size**: a 39× difference, invisible at any volume small enough to demo. **Sub-slice 5·2·1 built (backend) — tagging and coding, and the per-review-set access list the review-set model named and deliberately did not build.** Five per-firm tables in one migration (`20260808T000000_discovery-review-coding-and-access`, journal idx 51), the services and statement builders in `packages/discovery`, and fourteen routes in `apps/api-worker/src/routes/discovery-coding.ts`.

**The access list is the load-bearing half, and it is fail-closed.** No row means no access — an empty list is reachable by nobody rather than by everybody holding a discovery permission — so a bug in the seeding path hides a corpus instead of disclosing one, and only one of those two failures is the kind a person notices. **The predicate is composed in SQL, before the LIMIT, as a REQUIRED argument** to every statement builder that touches review-set content: a post-filter in the Worker would under-fill the page and turn the page size into an existence oracle for the rows it removed, and on a corpus whose whole point is that some people may not see it, that is the difference between a wall and a hint. A table-driven fitness pass enumerates every registered builder and asserts the marker is present, inside the `WHERE` clause and ahead of the `LIMIT`; a source scan proves the registry has not fallen behind the file it describes, and a behavioural pair proves the predicate actually excludes rather than merely appearing. A member not on a list gets a **404, never a 403** — "you may not see this one" names its existence. Widening a list requires `discovery:produce` and is audited; the last member cannot be removed, because under fail-closed an empty list is permanent short of a migration.

**Coding is per-document rows, always — family and bulk are scopes, not storage.** Applying to a family writes a row per member rather than one row members inherit, because inheritance resolved years later at production time is exactly where a bug becomes a produced privileged document; the event records the gesture, the rows record the result, and a production will read rows and only rows. **Single choice is structural, not guarded**: a partial unique index on `(document, group) WHERE removed_at IS NULL AND single_choice = 1`, with the group and cardinality denormalized onto the row precisely so the index can be written at all. Two concurrent writers cannot leave a document both responsive and non-responsive. **Rows are never deleted** — removal is a state with an actor and an instant, held by a CHECK that refuses half a removal. **Semantics, not names, drive the machine**: a closed vocabulary on the tag, so a firm renaming "Privileged" changes nothing, and a tag carrying one cannot be deactivated at all. Tags a firm creates carry none by design, so a renamed label can never change what a production withholds.

**Bulk freezes its selection before it writes anything** — resolved once through the access predicate, written to R2 under `selections/` (a record, not a cache, so it survives the review set closing), and walked. Criteria are recorded for humans and never re-run: a selection re-resolved per chunk tags documents the operator never saw. Chunks commit as several batches with the event in `running`, so a run that dies part-way leaves an honest partial rather than a silent one. **Undo is compensation and exact** — precisely the rows one act wrote and which are still live; a tag applied independently afterwards is untouched, a row already removed keeps its original attribution, and undoing a removal restores the original apply attribution behind two `NOT EXISTS` guards so a concurrent re-code wins rather than aborting. The undone act stays in the journal pointing at its reversal; an undo is itself an act and is not undone. **Coding writes no generic audit row**: the journal carries actor, instant, scope, criteria, frozen selection and reversal, and two homes for one fact drift. Panel and access-list changes are not coding decisions and do write one.

Progress counts and both quality-control reads ship: completion against the required questions, per-tag counts, the uncoded filter, and the **family-conflict read** — computed over the rows rather than stored, because a stored flag about two documents goes stale the moment either moves.

**Not built here and named.** The **UI is deferred to the owner** — the coding panel, tag chips on the list read, and the viewer pane are the surface this API is the backend half of, and the list read they page through is 5·1·4's. **Criteria-driven bulk at corpus scale** (everything matching a search, walked by a coordinator across turns) likewise waits on that index read; the materialized-selection contract is written so the criteria source is opaque to the executor, which is what lets it land without changing anything below it. Bulk today takes an explicit selection bounded by the same wall a load selection is. The **load profile** is 5·1·4's and stays `todo`.
